analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional maps with independent commissions and bans mid-decade redistricting.
analysis.headline: The bill, with only two Senate sponsors, never got a hearing or vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar states from redrawing congressional districts more than once after each ten-year census, except when a court orders it. It would require every state to hand map-drawing to an independent commission whose members cannot have held office or worked for a party or campaign, with all meetings open to the public and every draft map posted online. If the commission's plan was not enacted, courts would pick or draw the map instead of legislators.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, especially in states where legislatures redraw maps to protect the party in power or protect individual incumbents. The bill forces mapmakers to ignore voters' party affiliations and where incumbent House members live, and gives ordinary citizens notice, public hearings, interactive mapping software, and a way to submit their own plans. It would also stop mid-decade redistricting, the practice of redrawing maps between censuses for partisan gain.

how_it_helps.text: After each apportionment, a state may be redistricted only once, and only if a court orders a second round to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act [S2][S3].
Each state must establish an independent commission with balanced representation from the two largest parties in each legislative chamber, chaired by someone chosen by the other members [S2][S3].

Commission members cannot have held public office, run for office, or worked for a party or campaign in the prior four years, and must pledge not to run for Congress until after the next apportionment [S3].
Mapmakers may not consider voters' party affiliation, voting history, or the residences of incumbent House members, except as required by the Voting Rights Act [S2][S3].

All commission meetings must be public, and the state must run a website with precinct-level data, interactive software for citizens to draw their own plans, and a way to submit comments and plans [S3].

If the legislature does not enact the commission's plan, the state's highest court picks one, or a federal district court draws the map; legislators can approve or reject a commission plan but cannot amend it [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent House members and the legislative majorities of both parties, who lose the power to draw the districts they run in. States also bear the cost of running commissions, offset by a federal payment of $150,000 per congressional seat, authorized to be appropriated from the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbents who draw their own maps

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state procedures: a legislature could only approve a commission's plan or reject it, never amend it, and if a state fails to establish a commission a federal district court draws the map, which supporters of state control would object to as a federal takeover of a task the Constitution leaves largely to states [S3].

Commission members are appointed by legislative leaders of the two largest parties, so the design still routes picks through politicians, and a commission balanced between two parties can end up entrenching both parties' safe seats rather than creating competition [S3].
The ban on considering voting history and party affiliation could complicate compliance with the Voting Rights Act, though the bill carves out an exception where necessary to comply with it [S3].
It applies only to redistricting after the 2020 census, so it would not have affected any maps in force when it was proposed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but narrow: voters gain maps drawn by balanced, restricted commissions with open process, at the cost of removing discretion from state legislatures and adding federal oversight and roughly $150,000 per seat in federal spending. The main honest concern is that commission design matters enormously — this one keeps appointment power with legislative leaders of both major parties, which can produce maps that protect incumbents of both parties. Still, it addresses a concrete self-dealing problem: elected officials drawing the districts they run in.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2014, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Johnson of South Dakota introduced the Fairness and Independence in Redistricting Act on September 18, 2014, with Senator Mark Udall of New Mexico as cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never considered it, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

Because of its effective-date provision, the bill would only have governed redistricting after the 2020 census, giving states time to prepare but leaving all maps drawn after the 2010 census untouched [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislative majorities of both parties, who kept the power to draw congressional districts. Both parties' map-drawers were better off with the bill dead; no voter gains anything from it failing.

for.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chair: Sen. Patrick Leahy)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats, and the record shows no Republican or additional support; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Incumbent House members and state legislative majorities (the parties that control map-drawing)
industries.note: The bill removes their power to draw the districts they and their colleagues run in, bans considering incumbent residences and party affiliation, and outlaws mid-decade map redraws. Their interest in keeping that power runs against voters who currently have little say over district lines.
